opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been really interesting to watch. When we first put out the early state space work, and then Mamba, a lot of the reaction was academic curiosity: "Okay, this is a neat alternative to attention, but will it actually hold up at scale?" Over the last couple of years that's shifted quite a bit.

What I'm seeing now is that adoption isn't really "state space models replace transformers." It's much more about hybrids. A lot of the strongest production models mix a majority of SSM or linear-recurrent layers with a smaller number of attention layers. That combination gives you most of the efficiency benefits, like linear scaling in sequence length, constant memory during generation, and much higher inference throughput, while the attention layers handle the precise retrieval and copying that pure recurrent models can struggle with. Empirically, these hybrids often match or beat pure transformers on quality while being a lot cheaper to serve.

Inference cost is really what's driving it. As people push toward long context, agents that run for many steps, reasoning models that generate huge numbers of tokens, and multimodal inputs like audio, video, and genomics, the KV cache of a transformer becomes a real bottleneck. A model with a fixed-size state is just a much better fit for those workloads. So I think the economics are pulling the industry in this direction, even when the people adopting it don't think of themselves as "SSM people."

There's still friction. The transformer ecosystem has years of tooling, kernels, serving infrastructure, and institutional knowledge behind it, and that inertia is real. People also have open questions about how these models behave in very long-context retrieval, how to fine-tune them well, and how to reason about their failure modes. Those are active research areas, and I think we're making good progress on them.

Longer term, I don't think the right framing is SSMs versus attention. It's about understanding the underlying principles: what it means to compress context into a state, when you need exact recall versus a compressed summary, and how to design architectures that make that trade-off deliberately. I expect future models to be built from a richer toolbox where state space layers are a standard component, the way convolutions and attention are today. In that sense, production adoption is happening somewhat quietly, through hybrid designs and efficiency-focused deployments, and I expect that trend to keep accelerating.

r001.rationale: Predicts that production adoption will accelerate and connects state-space models’ efficiency to long-context, agent, reasoning, and multimodal workloads.

r002.rationale: Describes production hybrids using SSM or linear-recurrent layers alongside attention, and expects state-space layers to become a standard part of a broader architectural toolbox.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that I think adoption is happening, but mostly not in the form people initially expected, which was "an SSM replaces the Transformer wholesale." What's actually happening is more of a hybrid story.

If you look at what's being deployed now, the pattern is a handful of attention layers interleaved with a majority of Mamba-style or linear recurrent layers. That started with things like Jamba from AI21, then NVIDIA's Nemotron-H work, and a lot of internal models at labs that never get published. The reason that's the winning recipe is pretty intuitive once you think about it. The recurrent layers give you constant memory per token and linear scaling in sequence length, which is where all the inference cost savings come from. But a small number of attention layers buys you back the things recurrence is genuinely worse at, like precise retrieval of a specific token from way back in the context. You get most of the efficiency and almost none of the quality gap.

And I'd say the main driver of adoption isn't really benchmark scores, it's the economics of inference. When you're serving long contexts, the KV cache is the thing that kills you. It grows with every token, it dominates memory, it limits batch size, and therefore throughput. A model that's mostly SSM layers has a fixed-size state, so you can serve longer contexts with more concurrent users on the same hardware. For agentic workloads, where you're doing many long multi-turn interactions, that math becomes very compelling. So I think the pull is coming from infrastructure teams as much as from research teams.

That said, there are real barriers. The biggest one is honestly just ecosystem inertia. The entire stack, from kernels to serving frameworks to quantization recipes to fine-tuning tooling, has been optimized for attention for the better part of a decade. Even when the research is clear, it takes time for vLLM-style serving systems, hardware vendors, and all the surrounding tooling to catch up. We've spent a lot of effort on the kernel side to make these models actually fast on real GPUs, because a theoretically linear-time algorithm that's poorly implemented loses to a quadratic one with great kernels.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's still a research question around what these models are fundamentally good and bad at. My own view is that the tradeoff is basically about compression. An SSM has to decide what to keep in its state, and a Transformer keeps everything. That makes recurrent models worse at some things, but I actually think it makes them better at others, especially when you push on representation and tokenization. A lot of my recent interest is in whether you can go further and have models operate on raw bytes or learn their own chunking of the input, because the fixed-state models are the ones that are natural for that. If that works out, it's not just a cheaper Transformer, it's a different kind of model with its own advantages.

So my rough forecast: over the next few years, I think "pure attention" becomes the exception rather than the default for large production models, and most frontier systems end up as hybrids with some flavor of recurrent or state-space layer doing the bulk of the work. The research question of whether you can get rid of attention entirely stays interesting, but production doesn't need the answer to that to benefit. The hybrid is already good enough to be the pragmatic choice.

r001.rationale: Predicts that state-space or recurrent layers will become common in production generative models, especially for long-context and agentic workloads where fixed-size state improves inference efficiency.

r002.rationale: Describes adoption using both Mamba-style and linear recurrent layers, and forecasts hybrids with some flavor of recurrent or state-space layer, indicating production architectures need not be limited to Mamba.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see adoption happen gradually, and probably through hybrid architectures first. You don’t have to replace every attention layer with a state space layer to get some of the benefits. You can combine them and make different tradeoffs around memory, throughput, and the model’s ability to retrieve information from its context.

One of the attractive properties of state space models is that, during generation, you can maintain a fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache. That can be useful for long sequences or applications where serving cost matters a lot. But that same compression creates a tradeoff: how much information from the past can the model preserve, and how precisely can it access it later?

So I’d expect adoption to be driven by particular workloads rather than a universal replacement of transformers. And architecture is only part of it. You also need efficient kernels, support in inference frameworks, and confidence that the models perform reliably on the tasks people actually care about. That engineering ecosystem will be a big part of what determines the pace.

r001.rationale: It predicts adoption will grow gradually, driven by particular workloads where state space models’ fixed-size generation state benefits long sequences or serving cost.

r002.rationale: It mentions hybrid architectures combining attention and state space layers, but does not say that production adoption may include state space architectures beyond Mamba.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still pretty early. There’s a lot of interest in state space models because of the efficiency advantages, particularly when you’re generating long sequences. You can keep a fixed-size state instead of maintaining a KV cache that grows with the context, and that can be attractive in production.

But efficiency is only one part of the decision. People also need the model quality, the training infrastructure, and the inference tooling to be there. Transformers have a very mature ecosystem, so a new architecture has to offer enough of an advantage to justify that switch.

My expectation is that we’ll see adoption first in places where those advantages really matter—long-context workloads, streaming applications, or settings with memory constraints. And it may be through hybrid models that combine state space layers with attention. I don’t think production adoption necessarily means replacing every transformer layer; it means finding the combination that gives you the best quality and efficiency for a particular application.

r001.rationale: It expects adoption first in long-context, streaming, and memory-constrained workloads, citing their efficiency advantages.

r002.rationale: It says adoption may come through hybrid models combining state-space layers with attention, indicating architectures beyond Mamba.
